Name: Joe Lawson
Question: Do you remember your first best friend from high school? What were they like? Are they still your friend today?
Answer: Yes, I do! His name is Allen, and we met in the First Grade. We went all the way through our high school graduation together. He immediately entered Christian ministry while I took the opposite direction for a few years. But, long story short, Our high school class started having class reunions every few years and we got back in touch. He’s a semi-retired church pastor in Tennessee, USA and I am also a semi-retired church pastor in Mississippi. We keep up on Fb, 70 years after we met!

Question: Where is my friends list on Facebook?
Answer: Click on Facebook, then click on the little “house building” in the topline. Then look in the left column that usually starts with your name and scroll, for “Friends” In your language. Click on that and choices will open. Click on “All Friends” to see the whole friends list. If you’re looking for a specific name, click on the magnifying glass icon beside the big blue “F” instead and enter their name in the provided space. Voila!

Question: Is there a link between having no friends and developing sociopathic tendencies?
Answer: I’m sure there’s a link between having no friends and developing sociopathic tendencies. There are no positive peer role models, so “everyone else must be jerks for not helping me when I needed it.” That would likely manifest itself in “my” outbursts of anger and resentment against society in general.

Name: Joe Lawson
Question: My social adaption or whatever is way too much. I practically become a clone of whoever I’m talking to. I imitate their faces and do things they do. How can I stop this?
Answer: I once attended a 2-week class in Manufacturing Cost Estimating in Minneapolis, Minnesota; far north of my almost lifelong residence in Tennessee and then in Mississippi. I kept my mouth mostly shut when I was around all of the northerners who made up the rest of the class until the last day when we were waiting for the courtesy van to take some of us to the airport. I was dressed in my traveling jeans, and a sweatshirt and one of the others asked me where I lived. I answered, Mississippi. They all looked surprised and some said, “You sure don’t sound like you’re from the South.” I replied in an exaggerated drawl, “Yew meen Ah doan soun lak Ah ain’t frum aroun heah? Wail, it’s cause sum fokes mite pick awn me, liak we’uns do y’all when yewr daon thar.” And I switched back to, saying fast, “I pick up local dialects very quickly. It’s a form of protective coloration, like chameleons.” To answer your question, you can be yourself when you want to be — if you can remember who you are, anyway.

Question: How can I reduce the amount of time think about someone? I am friends with someone online and want to be, however, I think about them way too much. I message them and expect an answer right away whereas other friends I can wait days more detail below
Answer: I read your question, comment and more. It’s called a crush. It doesn’t have to be male or female. A crush is affection then desire raised to obsession with someone. The cure is to immerse yourself in something else you really enjoy doing to do, preferably with your brain and eyes. Just do things that you enjoy and which require your undivided attention.
